question: Norway has announced it will continue to develop new oil and gas resources in the Barents Sea, as it seeks to secure its contribution to European energy security. The EU’s 2021 Arctic policy, however, sets out a commitment to push for oil, coal and gas to remain in the ground, including in the Arctic, and to explore a multilateral obligation to prevent the development of new hydrocarbon reserves in the region.
Given that the Commission is currently updating this policy in the new geopolitical and geoeconomic context: 1.

What view does the Commission take of Norway’s plans to develop new oil and gas reserves in the Arctic in light of the EU’s current Arctic policy and its climate goals, including climate neutrality by 2050?
Does it consider replacing dependence on Russian fossil fuels with new investments that prolong Europe’s dependence on other hydrocarbons to be compatible with those goals?
When reviewing the EU’s Arctic policy, will the Commission continue to oppose the development of new hydrocarbon reserves in the region?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.11.2026) The Commission is in close and regular contact with Norway and has taken note of its positions on new hydrocarbon reserve development in the Arctic.

While Europe will still need declining quantities of fossil fuels during the transition from a diverse set of trusted partners, the EU’s ultimate objective is to remove any dependency on fossil fuels, for both climate and security reasons. Phasing out supplies from Russia, who has proven to be an unreliable partner, is a priority in that respect.

Through REPowerEU1, AccelerateEU2, the Electrification Action Plan3, the European Grids Package4, and many other efforts, the Commission continues its work of accelerating the transition to clean homegrown energy. The EU remains committed to the approach set out in the 2021 Joint Communication on the EU Arctic Strategy and will not support new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic5.

As set out in the Joint Communication on EU Arctic Policy adopted on 20 October 20266, the Commission will also work with partners to protect the Arctic environment and prevent all hydrocarbon reserve developments that pose a threat to the Arctic ecosystem.
